summary: Defines a CMS content type for the RPKI that carries a general-purpose list of checksums, called an RPKI Signed Checklist (RSC). It allows an attestation covering arbitrary files to be signed using specific Internet number resources. It is a standards-track specification.

plainLanguage.summary: You write a list of fingerprints for some files and sign it with a stamp proving you hold certain addresses. Anyone can check the files against it.

questions: what is an rpki signed checklist
how to sign files with rpki resources

how to verify files with rpki
subtitle: A way to sign a list of file checksums with your Internet number resources, so others can verify the files came from you.

tldr.problem: An organization that holds IP addresses or AS numbers sometimes needs to prove to another party that it produced certain files or data, and the RPKI had no general-purpose object for that.
tldr.mechanism: An RPKI Signed Checklist (RSC) is a CMS signed object that lists file names and checksums, marked with a set of Internet Number Resources and signed with a one-time-use EE certificate that covers those resources.
tldr.outcome: A relying party that validates the RSC can confirm that the holder of those resources produced the checklist, and then check any files against it. The RSC does not prove real-world identity.

facts.label: EE certificate use
facts.value: One RSC per certificate and key pair

today: RFC 9323 is a Proposed Standard published in November 2022. It has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: What an RSC Is For
sections.content:
RFC 9323 defines a Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) content type for a general-purpose listing of checksums, called a checklist, for use with the Resource Public Key Infrastructure (RPKI). The result is an RPKI Signed Checklist (RSC): a checksum listing signed with a specific set of Internet Number Resources.

When an RSC validates, it confirms that the holder of those resources produced it. The RFC expects this to help inter-domain business cases that depend on verifying resource holdership, such as automated Bring Your Own IP (BYOIP) on-boarding or establishing physical interconnections between Autonomous Systems.

The idea borrows from Resource Tagged Attestation (RTA), Manifests (RFC 9286) and OpenBSD's signify utility. The main difference from RTA is that RTA lets multiple signers attest one object, while an RSC lets a single signer attest many objects. The RFC treats the single-signer design as a simplification for implementers and operators.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine you want to prove to a friend that a stack of papers came from you. You write a list of fingerprints of the papers and sign it with a stamp only you own. An RSC does that for files, using Internet addresses as the stamp.

sections.title: Profile, Distribution and EE Certificates
sections.content:
An RSC follows the Signed Object Template for the RPKI (RFC 6488) with one exception. RSCs MUST NOT be distributed through the global RPKI repository system, so the Subject Information Access (SIA) extension MUST be omitted from the RSC's X.509 End-Entity (EE) certificate.

How an RSC travels is deliberately left open. The RFC jokes that it might be a USB stick, a web interface secured with HTTPS, a PGP-signed email, a T-shirt printed with a QR code, or a carrier pigeon.

The Certification Authority (CA) MUST sign only one RSC with each EE certificate and MUST generate a new key pair for each new RSC. This is the one-time-use EE certificate described in RFC 6487.
sections.plainLanguage: Each RSC gets its own brand-new stamp that is used once and never again. How you hand the signed list to someone is up to you.

sections.title: The RSC Content
sections.content:
The content type is id-ct-signedChecklist, with Object Identifier 1.2.840.113549.1.9.16.1.48. That OID MUST appear both in the eContentType of the encapContentInfo object and in the ContentType signed attribute of the signerInfo object.

The content, RpkiSignedChecklist, has four parts:

  • version: MUST be 0.
  • resources: the Internet Number Resources used to mark the attestation. They MUST be a subset of the resources on the EE certificate, and at least one of asID or ipAddrBlocks MUST be present.
  • digestAlgorithm: the hash used for the listed objects. It MUST be a hashing algorithm defined in RFC 7935.
  • checkList: one or more FileNameAndHash entries, one for each digital object.

The resource types are built to be binary compatible with the ASIdentifiers and IPAddrBlocks of RFC 3779, but are stricter. For IP addresses there MUST be only one entry per Address Family Identifier, ordered by ascending address family (so IPv4 comes before IPv6), and a Subsequent Address Family Identifier octet MUST NOT be present. Implementations MUST NOT ignore decoding errors from these stricter rules; such errors cause validation to fail.
sections.plainLanguage: The signed list says which Internet addresses or numbers the signer is using, which fingerprint method was used, and then a list of file names with their fingerprints.

sections.title: The Checklist Entries
sections.content:
Each FileNameAndHash pairs the name of a directory entry with the message digest of the digital object. The hash field is mandatory. The fileName field is OPTIONAL, so that an RSC can be used "stand-alone", with nameless objects addressed directly by their digest.

If a fileName is present, it MUST use only characters from the Portable Filename Character Set defined in POSIX, and it MUST be unique among the entries that have a name. If it is omitted, the hash MUST be unique among the entries that also lack a name.
sections.plainLanguage: Each line on the list has a fingerprint and, if you like, a file name. Two named lines cannot share a name.

sections.title: Validating an RSC and Checking Files
sections.content:
Before a Relying Party (RP) uses an RSC to check files, it MUST validate the RSC. That means all the checks in RFC 6488, except that the SIA extension MUST NOT be present in the EE certificate. On top of that:

  1. The eContent MUST conform to all the constraints of the RFC, including those for FileNameAndHash.
  2. If asID is present, the AS identifier delegation extension MUST be in the EE certificate, the listed AS identifiers MUST be a subset of it, and it MUST NOT contain "inherit" elements.
  3. If ipAddrBlocks is present, the same rules apply with the IP address delegation extension.

To verify a file, the RP computes its digest with the digestAlgorithm and compares it with the hash of the entries. At least one entry MUST match. Verification then runs in one of two modes. In filename-aware mode (the file has a name), exactly one matching entry MUST carry a file name equal to the object's name. In filename-unaware mode, exactly one matching entry MUST have no file name. Otherwise verification MUST fail and the error SHOULD be reported to the user.

The checklist may be longer than the set of files being checked, but implementations SHOULD warn the user in that case.
sections.plainLanguage: To check a file, you make its fingerprint again and look for it on the signed list. If the list's stamp is bad, or the fingerprint is missing, the check fails.

sections.title: Operational Notes
sections.content:
For plain-text objects such as ASCII, UTF-8, HTML, Javascript and XML, the RFC RECOMMENDS converting them to a lossless compressed form, for example GZIP. A compression envelope helps avoid unexpected canonicalization at intermediate systems, which would otherwise cause checksum errors. Validators treat a checksummed object as a string of arbitrary single octets.

If a listed file name matches no object being verified, a validator SHOULD compare every object's digest with that entry's hash and report matches to the user for consideration.
sections.plainLanguage: Packing text files in a zip-like wrapper keeps anyone along the way from changing small things, like line endings, that would change the fingerprint.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The data in an RSC is self-asserted. RPs MUST NOT assume anything about the signer beyond the fact that it had sufficient control of the issuing CA to create the object. The CA that issued the certificate has not verified the contents. RPKI certificates are not bound to real-world identities (see RFC 9255), so RPs need an outside authority to tie resources to a real entity.

Because RSCs are not published in the RPKI repository system, third parties may not know one exists. An observer might guess from gaps in EE certificate serial numbers, or from an unmatched serial number on a Certificate Revocation List, but the RFC says it is not possible to confidently infer the existence or non-existence of RSCs from repository state.

Finally, CAs are technically not prevented from signing several RSCs with one key pair, but RSCs that share an EE certificate cannot be revoked individually.
sections.plainLanguage: The signature shows the signer owns the Internet addresses. It does not say who the signer really is, and anyone with those addresses could make a signed list.

sections.title: IANA Actions
sections.content:
IANA allocated decimal 48, id-ct-signedChecklist, in the S/MIME CMS Content Type registry, and decimal 73, id-mod-rpkiSignedChecklist-2022, in the S/MIME Module Identifier registry. It also registered the OID in the RPKI Signed Objects registry as "Signed Checklist".

The file extension .sig was added to the RPKI Repository Name Schemes registry, and the media type application/rpki-checklist was registered, with binary encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: The official number registries were updated so the new kind of signed list has its own code, file ending and media label.

items.title: resources
items.text: AS numbers and/or IP addresses; a subset of the EE certificate's resources.

items.title: digestAlgorithm
items.text: A hash algorithm defined in RFC 7935.

items.title: checkList
items.text: One or more entries of optional file name plus hash.
